title: Discussion: Pre-Training Generative AI Models
html:
This discussion area is an additional means to interact with the weekly discussion and interactions. Please feel free to discuss our weekly topic live during the class session, via teams during the session, and/or here at any time during the week.

Additionally, groups can choose to present their weekly homework topics here if they choose to do so.

  1. Before the first meeting of the week:
    • Provide a substantive post reflecting on the reading materials and slide deck:
      1. One concept that was interesting to you and how you can apply it to your future career or life.
      2. One concept that was difficult to understand and what made it confusing.
      3. One external resource you found that helped you understand the concept better, along with an explanation of how it helped.
    • (Optional) Contribute to the group aspect of the weekly assignment.
  2. After the first meeting and before the second meeting of the week:
    • View and respond to the course recording.
    • Provide a written version of the in-class activities prior to the second meeting of the week AND
    • Respond to at least one peer to continue the conversation, clarify an idea, or share a relevant resource (you can respond to live session discussion points or online posts).
  3. Complete the weekly assignment.

Weekly Discussion Prompts: Pre-Training Generative AI Models

Use the prompts below to anchor your initial post, guide group collaboration, or prepare your responses:

Prompt 1: The Raw Web and Data Quality Filtering

  • Context: Foundational LLMs are pre-trained on trillions of tokens scraped from the public web (Common Crawl, Reddit, Wikipedia, GitHub). However, the vast majority of web text is low quality, duplicated, spam-ridden, or toxic.
  • Discussion Question: If you were designing the data curation pipeline for a new frontier LLM, what filtering heuristics, deduplication techniques, and quality classifiers would you prioritize? What are the risks of filtering out too much informal or non-standard language?

Prompt 2: Chinchilla Scaling Laws and Compute Optimization

  • Context: The Chinchilla scaling laws demonstrated that for optimal compute budget allocation, training token volume and parameter count should scale in roughly equal proportion, proving that many early models were severely undertrained.
  • Discussion Question: How did the shift toward 'overtraining' smaller models on massive token counts (e.g., Llama 3 training an 8B model on 15 trillion tokens) benefit deployment economics and edge devices?

Prompt 3: The Approaching 'Data Wall' and Synthetic Data

  • Context: Researchers estimate that high-quality human-generated text on the public internet will be exhausted within the next few years. Frontier labs are increasingly turning to synthetic data generated by other AI models to train future architectures.
  • Discussion Question: What is 'model collapse' when an AI trains on AI-generated data? How can developers generate high-quality synthetic reasoning curricula without causing models to degrade over recursive generations?

Prompt 4: Group Homework Topic Presentations (Optional)

  • If your group is choosing to present your weekly assignment findings here on the board, please share your slide link, code/workflow summary, and a brief overview of the problem you solved. Group members must reply within the thread to document individual contributions.
